text: Hide and seek, Dadda, cried Gip from a stool, and before I could stop them, the shopman brought a big drum down over him. <break time="0.8s" /> I shouted at him to take it off, but when he lifted it, the drum was empty, and the stool was empty too. <break time="0.8s" /> There is no deception, sir, he said once again, and then he slipped quickly away through a dark doorway. <break time="0.8s" /> I leaped after him, and the next moment I bumped into a working man in the bright daylight of Regent Street. <break time="0.8s" /> It was Gip himself who stood beside me, holding four parcels, and he quietly took hold of my finger again. <break time="0.8s" /> Where the shop had been, I saw only a plain pillar between a picture shop and a window full of baby chicks. <break time="0.8s" /> In the cab, I threw away a glass ball that I found in my pocket, and Gip said at last, Dadda, that was a proper shop. <break time="0.8s" /> At home, the parcels held three boxes of ordinary lead soldiers and a white kitten, which was very much alive. <break time="0.8s" /> Months later, Gip told me that his soldiers did march by themselves whenever he said the word, but I have never seen them move. <break time="0.8s" /> I have never found that shop again, but I suppose the bill will come someday, since they know Gips name and address.
